questions.q: A dataset is 95% negative. A model that always predicts negative scores what accuracy?
options: About 95%, while finding no positives at all
questions.explain: Predicting the majority class is right for every negative row, so accuracy equals the majority share. That is why a dummy baseline is the number to beat.

questions.q: In the lesson the logistic regression had 97% accuracy and 44% recall. What does the recall tell you?
options: It found fewer than half of the actual positives
It is wrong 44% of the time
The test set was too small
questions.explain: Recall is the share of actual positives caught. At 0.439 the model missed more than half of them, which accuracy alone hid.

questions.q: Why pass stratify=y to train_test_split on imbalanced data?
options: It makes the model train faster
It keeps the class ratio the same in the train and test parts, so the test set always contains positives
questions.explain: Stratified splitting preserves proportions. A plain split of a rare class can leave the test set with too few positives, or none.

questions.q: What precision does a random guesser achieve on the rare class?
options: Roughly the positive rate of the data
questions.explain: If you flag rows at random, the share of flagged rows that are truly positive equals the base rate, here about 0.053. That is the dashed baseline on the precision-recall plot.

questions.q: Which set of measures is best for judging a model on 5% positive data?
options: Recall, precision, average precision, and a business cost
questions.explain: These focus on the rare class or on real costs. Accuracy is dominated by the majority class and can look excellent for a useless model.
